I did not say that.

I am willing to admit that the hon. gentleman's scheme is ahead of many others that are being put forward by different members of the government. Look at what the Canadian Pacific Railway are doing to-day. It is doing just what American railway and shipping companies have done for the last twenty years in the United States. These American interests have placed on the Great Lakes the largest possible vessels to carry grain to Buffalo, where it is placetU'on the best systems of railways that money can produce that carry il at rates that beat the Welland canal. The Canadian Pacific Railway is undertaking an expenditure probably running to $10,000,000 to secure a lake port on Georgian bay at Victoria harbour, a few miles below Midland. They are constructing their line from that point to Peterborough. This will give them an all-rail route from Victoria harbour to Montreal, which is their Atlantic shipping point. The Grand Trunk are spending as much at Midland. Tliey are building extensive docks and also an elevator that will make this little elevator at Port Colborne a mere trifling affair. And the Canadian Pacific Railway are constructing one of about equal importance at Victoria harbour. The public wonder, when they hear the ministers of this government put forward their schemes, how these railway companies, having immense interests behind them, and headed .by men of such eminent ability as Sir Thomas Shaug-nessy and Mr. Hays, can ask of their stockholders to provide these millions upon millions of dollars to construct their transportation schemes. And the general public are simply laughing at the government.
But they are laughing in rather a serious way when they consider the proposals the government are putting forth. Nothing need be said about the Port Colborne scheme, where three and a half million dollars have gone, and that is all going to be an experiment. Even if it were finished, vessels carrying 70,000 bushels of grain would go right past there to Kingston-I have heard that opinion expressed by capable vessel men. My hon. friend admits that a vessel carrying 80,000 bushels gets as much per bushel as a vessel carrying
400.000	bushels. I am free to admit that a
400.000	bushel vessel makes more money for her proprietors ; but there is the fact that the smaller vessels of 70,000 or 80,000 bushels get the same rates as the larger vessels of 400,000 bushels. Vessel men claim that they have been making 20 per cent in this business.
But look at the superiority of the Georgian Bay plan over the Buffalo plan. Buffalo to-ciav controls the trade, reaching to 300.000,000 bushels of grain every year. Where is your Welland canal service com-

pared with that ? A mere bagatelle is that which goes down the Welland canal compared with that which goes via Buffalo. But let the minister and the House remember this, that once the Canadian Pacific Railroad and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have all their terminal facilities completed at Midland and Victoria Harbour, and have their lines of railway running to Peterborough and Port Hope where they will strike their main lines, when they will be able to run 50 cars per train instead of 17, they will be able to beat the Buffalo trade out. And why ? Because they will make three trips to Midland or to Victoria as against two to Buffalo from the upper lake ports. Ask any vessel men if these figures are correct, and they will tell you they are. To-day you can, with the same vessel, make three trips to .Midland as against two to Buffalo. That is an enormous advantage, when you consider that these vessels can carry 400,000 bushels of grain, and that the rate in the fall of the year sometimes runs up to three cents a bushel. When the Canadian Pacific Railway works are built at Midland and Victoria Harbour, the same vessel going to those ports will make $12,000 on three trips, more than if she was employed in the trade to Buffalo. Now I would advise the minister to go slow, and let the country have a chance to breathe for a while and see whether the m-ojects of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific are going to be a success, and whether this Port Colborne proposal is going to aid the Welland canal. Let the Minister of Railways and Canals take the advice of his former colleague, Mr. A. G. Mackay, who characterized the government of Mr. Whitney as spending the money of the province like a lot of drunken sailors. The phrase was expressive, if not elegant. But think of the few thousands being spent in the province of Ontario compared with the threatened expenditure of millions coming on top of that. Here is this terrible expenditure, this awful expenditure, that is going to drag down Canada for years to come,, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, that is going to cost the country-every man sees it-not a hundred millions, but it will never be completed for $200,000,000. And coming on top of that huge expenditure, what do we see ? The government threatens now to plunge Canada into an expenditure for building a Hudson Bay Railway, and a canal from the Georgian Bay. In the name of ail that is good let the country have a rest for a little while, and let the private enterprise of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway who are to-day expending millions of dollars, in conjunction with the projects that the government has now undertaken at Port Colborne, have a chance to develop themselves, and don't drive the people of Canada into a state of eonsterna-Mr. BENNETT	.
tion by threatening to unsettle the financial conditions of the country.

So far as I am concerned, I have every session advocated the enlargement of thp Welland canal, and I think that is one of the most important public works that this government could undertake. When the Welland canal was first enlarged to 14 feet it was supposed that would be sufficient depth for many years to come. But what is the case to-day ? We all see that vessels carrying 300,000 bushels and over are navigating the lakes. My idea is that these large vessels will seek the very nearest point on the sea-board. Today the minister admits that the amount of money the government are expending for the Port Colborne elevator, $732,000, is to be practically wiped out, and will be absolutely useless, if he goes on and constructs the Welland canal as he has been telling the people he proposes to do. Of course he understands that these large vessels will never stop to unload at Port Colborne, so that port will practically be abandoned. Now at the present time grain is being carried, I may say, for 3J cents a bushel from Port Arthur right through to Montreal, that is the nresent rate, the summer rate ; but in the fall it is 5 cents a bushel. Now I claim that when that Welland canal is deepened to 25 feet, as the minister states, these large vessels carrying 300,000 or 400,000 bushels will go either to Kingston or to rrescott. I say Prescott, because it is at the foot of navigation, and grain will be taken from either Kingston or Prescott to Montreal for one cent a bushel. That can be done, these large vessels will bring that grain from Port Arthur to Prescott for a cent and a half a bushel. If these vessels carrying 65,000 bushels will take grain from Port Arthur to Montreal for 31 cents, which means practically 2i to Prescott, there is no reason that I can see why they would not bring grain for lj cents to Prescott or to Kingston.
How long does it take an ordinary vessel carrying 70,000 bushels to lock through the Welland canal at present ? It takes fully 18 hours.
It takes 16 hours.

Admitting it takes 18 hours to do the locking now, and the present rate of grain is'3J cents a bushel from Port Arthur delivered into the ocean steamers at Montreal, if the ocean steamers are in a position to take it out of the vessel, then, even if the Welland canal is enlarged, they will bring it down to Prescott for 1J cents a bushel. I claim that if the government, instead of undertaking that Port Colborne elevator, had undertaken the enlargement of the Welland canal, as they propose now, that money would have been put into a work that would have been of

use for all time to come. I hope that the enlargement of the Welland canal will be proceeded with at the earliest possible moment. X believe that it is in the interest of the country that it should be done, and commenced at once, and X shall continue to advocate it, whether I am in the House or out of it.
Is it the purpose of the government to bring power there to run the elevator, and if so how much would it cost?
That deals with something I do not know much about. We made a contract for power to run the elevator at half a cent per kilowatt hour.
That is a contract entered into by the government?
Yes.
What is the estimate of the cost of running that elevator for the season?
The cost of running the elevator for the season will depend on the volume of grain passing through the elevator.

Suppose it runs up to its
800,000	bushels capacity?
That would simply be the capacity per day.
Suppose it keeps going to its full capacity what will the cost of running the elevator be.

I could not say. Half a cent per kilowatt hour is something that an electrical engineer has to figure out, but I can say that every electrical engineer with whom I have talked on this matter- and I have talked with many-said that it was the best contract for electrical power as far as the government is concerned that has ever been made. It was made with the Ontario Power Company. In operating an elevator of that kind the power has to be kept at what is always called the peak load. That means that there must always be sufficient power to run the elevator at its full capacity, whereas there may be days and days when the elevator would only be running at half its capacity. The electrical company is required to keep the power at a sufficient volume to run the elevator at its full capacity and it will only get paid for the actual amount of electrical power that is being used at any one time.
Convert that into ordinary horse-power, let us know what it costs and we will understand it.
It will be $11 or $12 per horsepower.

If you can let us know what it will cost to elevate 100,000 bushels
of grain you will come down to the understanding of ordinary mortals.
It is above me. The estimates made for the running of the elevator for seven months from the 1st of September to the 31st March next is $3,000, of which $1,600 will, we expect, be for power.
The government will be prepared to run the elevator and take in whatever grain comes?
Yes, beginning on the 1st September.
Is the government going to carry the grain?

That opens up a pretty big question to which I referred some months ago in this House. It is a debatable question whether the elevator should not be leased to a company that will fill and empty it for the benefit of the trade.

As has been stated by my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), this plant at Port Colborne has cost $3,500,000. It is almost ready for operation. My own opinion is that the best policy that the government could have pursued would have been to have deepened the Welland canal to 25 feet. However, this scheme was conceived at a time when a very large amount of wheat from the Canadian Northwest was going out by way of Buffalo, when large boats from the head of tne lakes were delivering this grain at Buffalo and some people, amongst them Mr. George Bertram, thought that we could divert that grain to the St. Lawrence by building this elevator at Port Colborne. I did not agree with him, but I believed that the best thing that could have been done was to have deepened the Welland canal, but the scheme was to try and encourage some of the vessel owners to carry out the system which was proposed at that time, that large barges should be employed to go as far as Port Colborne for cargo through this elevator-perhaps one steam barge towing two ordinary steel barges. It was thought that these barges could be towed down Lake Ontario and through the St. Lawrence canals. I think that is a scheme which should commend itself to the Montreal shipping firms. They have barges which go through the St. Lawrence canals and I think we ought to try and see if they will not send them as far as Port Colborne. The cost of elevating grain in such an elevator as this is very little indeed, and I am not sure but what this scheme of transporting grain from the head of the lakes to Montreal would be as economical a scheme as any we have at the present time. I do not think it would be as cheap as to transport grain from the head of the lakes to Prescott and Kingston, by the Welland canal route, it the Welland canal were deepened,

but it would be as cheap as any in existance at the present time. We have always contended In Canada that our canal systems have been regulators of freight rates, as they have contended in New York state that the Erie canal has been a regulator of freight rates. The Erie canal does not have the capacity of the St. Lawrence canals for carrying a large volume of traffic, but it has always been the regulator of freight rates, and they never would have got such a low rate on the New York Central for grain' going to the sea-board if it had not been for the Erie canal. I have very much the same criticism to make in regard to our transportation schemes ns ray lion, friend from East Simcoe made. It has been demonstrated that east of the lakes there is very little profit in carrying grain. Whatever profit there is in carrying grain is west of the lakes where the railway companies have more of a monopoly and they can regulate their rates to suit themselves to a greater extent. But once you land the grain at the head of the lakes, competition is very keen and there is very little money in carrying from that point.
You are speaking of through grain?
I am speaking of grain for export.
The rate on grain from points in my constituency to Montreal is greater than it is from' Fort William to Montreal.

I know that local rates are very much higher than through rates. That is another question that I do not intend to dwell upon just now, but I would like to invite the attention of the minister to the number of routes east of the lakes that we have in working order at the present time. First, I will refer to the American system of railways and transportation which routes are very numerous, which we all know about and which are an important factor with respect to competition. Then we have the Canadian Pacific Railway from Owen Sound to the sea-board and the" Canadian Pacific Railway from Victoria harbour to the sea-board, which has been re erred to by my hon. friend from East Simcoe. We have the Grand Trunk Railway from Depot Harbour, Parry Sound, Midland, Collingwood, Wiarton, Goderich, Sarnia and Windsor. We have the St. Lawrence canal system and we will have, I suppose, the Trent canal system. Then we have the system that we are referring to at the present time, and which is part of -the St. Lawrence canals system-the scheme of transferring grain at Port Colborne, taking it from large boats and putting it through the elevator. We have before us the Hudson Bay Railway. We have the Georgian Bay canal scheme and we have the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in the debate upon that1 Mr. KEMP.
scheme in this House we were told that the Grand Trunk Pacific would carry grain to the sea-board at a cheaper rate than it could be carried by any canal or railway in existence. It is on record in ' Hansard ' that ministers of the Grown made that statement when the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill was going through this House. We have also the Erie canal and the American transportation system. It seems to me that the time has come when we should call a halt. If we have money to spend and if money can be saved to the benefit of the farmers in the Northwest it seems to me that the very first thing that we should ascertain is whether or not we can save sufficient to warrant us in spending what will be required to deepen the Welland canal. That seems to be a feasible project, because if we can load these large vessels to carry half a million bushels of wheat as far as Kingston and Prescott, where it can be transferred to barges which would float down the river to Montreal- it would be as cheap to store the wheat in those barges as to put it into the elevator at Montreal-and if the wheat could then be transferred through floating elevators to the steamships at Montreal, it strikes me that it would have the effect of reducing the cost of carriage and of diverting a large amount of the grain trade to the St. Lawrence route. That, it seems to me, would be an inexpensive way by which the produce not only of the northwestern states, but of our own Northwest could be transported to the sea-board. We should not invest another dollar in any of these schemes before we have ascertained from experts what is the cheapest way of transporting a bushel of wheat from the head of the lakes to the sea-board.
These engineers' reports go for nothing in my mind. They gave us information as to what can be done and in these days of advanced engineering almost anything can be accomplished if you are willing to spend the money. If after the work is done you can carry a bushel of wheat a fraction of a cent cheaper by one route than by another, you can divert the traffic by that route. Although I am greatly in favour of the Welland canal route for many reasons, even in reference to it. I think that the only proper way to proceed is to have the opinion of experts as to whether grain can be carried to the sea-board by that route cheaper than by any other. I am thoroughly opposed to going into so many half digested schemes of transportation and talking big to the" people all over the country, trying to make them believe we are to deepen the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals and to have the Georgian Bay canal, when it is impracticable to do all these things, when we cannot afford them. Let us devote our attention to one scheme. A 25-foot Welland canal would be efficient to carry all the grain of the Northwest. But while doing

that we must not discourage private enterprise. I agree with the hon. member for Simcoe that the railways have done a great work. Let us improve the harbours on the Georgian bay and assist the railways, but we must remember that the Welland canal system is the regulator of freight rates to the sea-board.

The hon. gentlemen are developing a proposition that might have been much better discussed in the earlier days of the session when we had nothing to do. The policy of constructing an elevator and the deepening or practically building a harbour at Port Colborne was adopted by reason of the fact that the Welland canal as a portion of our transportation system was practically useless without the elevator and harbour. I supported the building of the elevator and the enlargement of the harbour because those two things were both necessary and will be necessary even after the Welland and St. Lawrence canals are deepened and the Georgian Bay canal is constructed. The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has made the assertion that I was opposed to the deepening of the Welland canal.
I did not say that.

I understood my hon. friend to make that statement and I think I am quite correct in my assumption. I think he made it. However, he is liable to develop erratic theories and to endeavour to square the facts to the theories. I am not opposed to the deepening of the Welland canal by any means. I think the Welland canal in the future will need to be deepened and enlarged to meet the future growth and development of this country, but at present we are dealing with a vote in connection with the completion of certain improvements at Port Colborne authorized by parliament. These improvements are necessary as a step towards the solution of the transportation problem of this country, they have been approved of in the past and I am sure will be found in the future to have been necessary and to justify the expenditure of this money.

I am glad to hear from the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) now that he is in favour of deepening the Welland canal, but in view' 'of what he says as to not speaking earlier in the session I would call attention to t,he fact that when the Georgian Bay canal scheme was under discussion I had the temerity to advocate the deepening of the Welland canal rather than the construction of the Georgian Bay canal and had not his support then.

Some remarks I had occasion to make in this House two or three years ago have been amply verified. I went into the matter of general transportation quite extensively and at that time I agreed
that the building of the elevator at Port Colborne would probably be of benefit. The idea seems to be to deepen the Welland canal very quickly. I do not think that we need be in a hurry about deepening the Welland canal for some years to come. We are only now getting the improved elevator system ready to work and we have had no demonstration as to what benefit we will derive from it. Then, again, suppose you deepen that Welland canal, is it going to be to the interest of Canadian trade or American trade? Will it draw away trade from Canadian channels? That is a matter that should be well considered. As soon as you deepen the Welland canal to 25 to 30 feet you open a clear waterway to all American corn, wheat and grain of any kind to Og-densburg or to any of the ports on Lake Ontario and that means that grain, which under the present arrangement will probably come largely to the elevator at Port Colborne would go down through the deepened Welland canal to American ports. For what reason? Suppose the large lake vessels could come down to-day from Duluth or Chicago and go through the Welland canal. They certainly would not go beyond Prescott. They would go where they could get a return cargo. As soon as they passed Port Colborne they would have to go to the American side for their return cargo, so they would carry their eastbound cargo there and take their return cargo back. Lgt us have a trial of the benefit that we have been expecting to derive from the elevator and improvements at Port Colborne before we undertake or put the country looking towards the deepening of the Welland canal. Let us have a trial of one, two, three or four years. That was the argument I made two or three years ago, but at the same time I advocated the postponement of the building of or agitation for the Georgian Bay canal until this route had become developed and we could see what it would do. Then you could put on a commission and ascertain what benefit you would receive from the building of the Georgian Bay canal system. In the meantime our railways would be developed just as they are being developed to-day, from Midland or from Tiffin or Depot Harbour or any of these ports. By that time probably we will have also the Grand Trank Pacific which road with a 4-10 grade can at the same rate as is charged by any other large grain carrying road of the northwest haul their grain from Winnipeg into Quebec a good deal cheaper or quite as cheaply as it can be carried by the rail and lake route. These are matters on which I hope the government will not lose their heads. When the time comes for the Georgian Bay canal then build it. I do not believe the time has come for it. IV hen the time comes to enlarge the Welland canal, do it. In the meantime I hope the government will give the improvements and the elevator and storage facilities at Port Col-

borne a thorough, complete trial so they will be able to demonstrate not only the cost but the question as to whether the grain will tend to come by way of Montreal or by way of Buffalo. We know well that the American shippers would prefer to ship by Montreal during summer the grain stored in Chicago. They will pay larger prices for shipment by Montreal than by the southern route. There is a large traffic which probably would not go through Montreal and neither would any of the other grain come through Montreal. We would not hope to develop a traffic from the United States by deepening the Welland canal, for then you would open the way to the New York terminus at cheaper rates probably than could possibly be given to Montreal. You must stop at either Port Colborne or Prescott. It will cost too much for many generations to deepen the St. Lawrence canals.

On the 11th June I asked for certain information with regard to the cost of the Mountain division of the National Transcontinental Railway A return has been brought hewn which is absolutely unsatisfactory, because 1 cannot understand what is intended. It is said that the length of the whole road from Winnipeg to the coast is 1,755 miles, of which 916 miles are included in the prairie'- section and 839 miles in the mountain section. Further down I find this language :
The estimated cost of construction is set down at the present date at $61,520,000, which includes terminals at Prince Rupert, $3,000.-1
000.
Does that refer to the mountain section or to the whole road from Winnipeg to the coast ?
That is the Mountain section.

Might I suggest to the minister that when his clerks prepare returns they make a matter of that kind plain, so that I need not take up the time of the House in asking questions which would be unnecessary if the return were brought down in proper form ?
Sault Ste Marie canal-construction, $105,000.
That is the amount expended in deepening and widening the Chanel at the upper end. Mr. Boone has the contract, amounting to $256,657.
How much has been paid on it?
$234,102 up to September of last year.
Has the contractor been paid the amount estimated, or does the government expect that the work will cost more than the amount of the contract ?
This vote is expected to cover the whole amount Mr. J. T. SCHELL.
It is going to cost the country $50,000 more than the amount of the contract.
Although these contracts are made on an estimate of a lump sum, the payments are at schedule rates of so much a yard.
Has the minister's department had any expense in connection with the work at present being done by the American government at Lime Kiln crossing near Windsor ?
I think I am safe in saying no, but I will make inquiry.
Will the minister in-quix-e whether his department has in its employ a couple of agents superintending the operations of the American government ?,
Has the minister ever gone along the Rideau canal to see how it is lighted ?	'

The Rideau canal seems to be under double jurisdiction. Part of the wox-k is done by one department and part by another.
Mi-. J. D. REID. In going through that canal this summer I noticed that it is lighted by lanterns hanging from sticks.
That would be in the lake section.

Although the canal is supposed to be lighted every night, it seems to be lighted only about two nights in the week. Although there ai-e not many boats navigating the Rideau canal, I think in the interests of navigation it should be lighted every night.
Does the minister propose to make his statement to-night ?
I am not quite ready to make my statement to-night.

Can he say when he will make it ?
Mi\ GRAHAM. I will be prepared to take it up to-morrow.
I would also like to know when the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Box-den) proposes to make his statement. Will that be to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say. Mr. J. D. REID. He said he was ready.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then, I will ask him to be here to-morrow.
Then, we will take the Transcontinental first ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.

After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight oclock.
Quebec canals-steam road roller and stone crusher, $7,000.
What is this required for?

To macadamize the tow path. They do a great deal of travelling on the canal bank.
Soulanges canal-improvements, $15,000.
What are the improvements there ?

Fire protection, electric motors, machine shop, timber and lumber shop, cast-iron and concrete posts.
St. Lawrence canal-district office, $7,000.

This is really finishing up the expenditures for work in that district. We have our engineer and staff there.
Trent canal-construction, $1,000,000.
Is this work all under contract ?
Yes, all let to the lowest tenderers.
Has the southern outlet been determined upon yet ?
No.

I want to ask the minister with reference to that Devil's Elbow he has been talking about, that is, the work at Bradford. The minister explained the other day that the chief engineer is not able to attend to it now. Could not the minister send some one else up there in the meantime ?

I had a little conversation with the secretary of the chief engineer this morning, and I understood him that some time before the session closed lie thought he could give me an idea of win t that work was going to cost. I think lie said some engineer was there looking at it.

I think the chief engineer is quite familiar with the general character of the situation. It is absolutely level land, it is called a marsh. I was at Bradford the other day, and talking with a gentleman who knows a great deal about it in a nonprofessional way, he said the distance was about three-quarters of a mile. The soil is mucky on top for about three feet, then you get to solid earth. I would be glad if the minister, before the session closes, would give me an idea as to whether he will undertake the work.
I wall try and get that.

It is a place where there will ba a good deal of traffic, which comes up to the point of the Devil's Elbow. It is a small matter, and will give an additional
outlet to the people of Bradford and of the neighbourhood.
Could the minister tell me when the contract was let for the section passing through the town of Campbellford ?
I cannot say that. When the work of the session is over and my chief engineer comes back, I intend to go with him to see the place.
Will this complete the Trent canal ?

The Trent canal will not be completed until it has got away up into the waters of Lake Simcoe. There are some sections of it for which an estimate has not yet been made. I have sent out for information on those sections which are under contract.
How many years will it take to complete the canal, and how much will it cost ?
If we base an estimate for the future on the number of years it has been going on, some of us will be pretty old men when it is completed.
Then it won't be any benefit to this generation ?

I think it is a great accommodation now.
Lachine canal-wall north side basin No. 2, $98,000; wall side basin No. 2, $49,000; workshops, $15,000.

Does that finish the
wall on basin No. 2?
Yes.
How much does the whole wall cost?

$147,000. It is under
contract.
Chambly canal-to macadamize towpath, to complete, $10,000.
What do those macadamized roads cost altogether?
$3,500 a mile, and there are four or five miles.
Will the stone crusher and roller be utilized here ?

Yes.
Cornwall canal-to build a gate lifter, $10,-
000.
What does that gate lifter cost altogether?
Murray canal-to provide houses for bridge-men, $5,000.
What kind of houses, and how many?

There are eight men and only two houses, and the whole length of the canal is several miles away from any town. We propose to build two houses one and a half stories each, at $2,500 each.
Rideau. canal improvements, $1,500.
What are the improvements?

Building a platform and rebuilding the swing bridge across the upper lake.
Trent canal improvements, $45,000.
What are those improvements?
Dredging between Bob-caygeon and Peterborough, Peterborough and Fenelon, and Balsam lake and Lake Simcoe. We do that with our own dredge.
Are you getting a dredge built for that?

We propose to get one built. $15,000 is the estimate.
Trent canal-new lock and dam, Lindsay, $80,000.
We are replacing the old wooden locks which the Ontario government built there some fifty years ago.
Will that be used in the navigation of the Trent?

Yes.
Trent canal-dam at Buckhorn, $25,000.
This work is being done by Conroy, of Peterborough, and was let by tender. The amount is $55,119.
Is it intended to place the section under contract between Lake Simcoe and the Georgian bay this coming year?
Not this season.
Where is the dam at Buck-horn being built, and what is it for?

It is for navigation purposes practically, and we imay develop power as well.
Intercolonial Railway-increased accommodation at Halifax, $500,000.
The departmental report says that three contracts were let at Halifax during the year. Who are the contractors and what is the contract price in each case?
The contract for grading on the west side of water street is not a lump sum contract but is a contract at schedule prices.
Who is the contractor ? Mr. GRAHAM. Kitchen & Co.
Has the minister a statement of the estimated value of the contract ?
I do not seem to have it here. The estimated expenditure is about $520,000 for the year. The expenditure to the 31st March last was $3,233,158.01.
Has the minister a list of the amounts paid under each of the contracts ?
No, I will try and get a statement of the different contracts.
The report states that the Cunard property was secured by the railway. I would like to know what was paid for that.
Through whom was the purchase negotiated ?
There was an offer made, arbitrators were appointed and it was settled by the officers of the department.
Did Mr. Mcllreith get a fee ?	%
Mr. Mcllreith searched the title or did some legal work of that kind.
What was the amount of his fee for that service ?
Has my hon friend a copy of the Public Accounts ?

There does not seem to be anything in the Public Accounts. All I find in the Auditor General's Report is the amount paid to Kitchen & Co. for excavation. There seems to have been $54,217.51 paid out during the last fiscal year on account of the Halifax works.

Would the minister state what he intends this $500,000 shall be applied to, whether it will meet the object be has in view, and what is the total amount that lias been expended for increased accommodation at Halifax ?

The amount expended to the end of March is $3,233,000 in round numbers. This amount is required for additional facilities on the west side of Water street, engine house, heating and turntable, freight and car repair shoxi and planing mill, store house, oil house and sand house, chimney and foundation. coal pockets, water tank and supply, cinder pits, grading, ballasting and tracks, double tracking Richmond to new yard, beating of buildings, &e., tracks and turnouts in Richmond yard, building for car inspectors and wharf. These improvements which I am speaking of now will cost $1,019.80.
Which, added to $3,200,000 will be $4,200,000 ?
$4,255,000. But the $3,200.000 includes the $500,000 already expended.
I notice, at page W-19 of the Auditor General's Report that Mr. R. T. Mcllreith, for legal services and expenses, received $1,861.30. Was that in connection with the purchase of property in Halifax ?
This was in connection with the purchase of property required for these improvements.
Did this include the properties in connection with which Mr. Pearson got $14,000 ?
The last item, in connection with the roundhouse, I think is the only one.
Is any of this expenditure for increased accommodation at Halifax charged to revenue account besides what is charged to capital ?

No, I think not, this is revolutionary.
Sydney Mines-extension to, $14,625.

This is from North Sydney to Sydney Mines, not quite three miles, 2 7 I think. It is an extension of the line. The expenditure up to March 31, 1907, was $88,043. That includes the land and a very large yard to accommodate the traffic we receive from the Nova Scotia Coal Company.
Improvements at North Sydney, $4,000.

That is an addition to the engine house.
Mr, HAGGART. Why is that Charged to capital account ?

It is really a new thing, to provide accommodation for more engines, we might have built it by itself and it would then have been absolutely new but we attached it to the other one.
Sydney-increased accommodation, $14,000.

This is in connection with the bridge at Sydney yard. The bridge itself will cost about $14,000.
Improvements at Mulgrave, $1G,800.

This is to provide an extension of the wharf, additional sidings, extension of the freight shed, land, coaling pockets, improvements at the station and water tank. The total cost will be $78,800. This vote finishes the work.
Antigonish-increased accommodation, $4,500.

We are building a concrete platform, providing drainage and completing the water service ; the work is practically finished. I received a telegram today asking me to extend the work to the
amount of $400 in order to have our walk meet the town walk. If we decide to do that we will require $400 more. We have expended there $21,354.57. It is under contract to Mr. Sutherland.
New Glasgow-increased accommodation, $7,500.

This is to complete the work of providing two undercrossings. The expenditure to March 31, 1907, was $46,677.22.
Stellarton-increased accommodation, $6,500.

This is for a sand house and electric lighting plant. It will take about $9,000 more to complete this work. It is under contract. The General Electric Company are putting in the lighting plant.
Pictou-increased accommodation, $8,600.
Is any of this sum for Pictou to be applied to the contract for the engine house ?
There is nothing in this. It is for coaling pockets, water service, loading platform and a building for our car cleaners.

In connection with the contract for the Pictou engine house I was informed some time ago by the minister that the contract was $13,950, that there were some schedule prices, and that the contractor had been paid to that date $M0,-221 and that there was a final estimate amounting to $10,719 remaining to be paid, so that the total amount payable to the contractor would be about 111,000. How is it that such a large sum has been paid under that contract ? The department estimated the value of the contract at $62,000. The contractor Mr. Walberg, has received nearly double that amount.
What Is the estimate upon which the contract was made, what is the amount expended, and what do you require to finish the work ?
This work is all finished and paid for.

It is true that the contract for the building proper was $13,950, but the department estimated the contract upon Mr. Walberg's tender of schedule prices and including the bulk sum as worth $62,000. Notwithstanding that, we find that he received over $110,000 on that contract. It seems that In this case, as in all other cases in which contracts were awarded to Mr. Walberg, he was the lowest tenderer, but he managed to come out at the completion of this contract as in the case of all his other contracts with an amount far in excess of the highest tender. I can understand that there might be some slight variation between the department's estimate and the actual working out of the contract; but it does seem to me that it is not very complimentary to the engineering staff of the Department of Railways and Canals that they should be out to such an immense extent as in this case. There were additional amounts in connection with the Pic-tou engine house outside of Mr. Walberg's contract which made the total value of this work $129,111. It is an Immense amount of money to spend for such an engine house as that at Pictou.

My hon. friend is wrong. This item has nothing at all to do with the item he is discussing. The details of this contract will appear in the Auditor General's Report for the year just past. The contract was for an engine house, crib-work, and several other things ; but as it is not a matter germane to this item, I did not bring the details.
Mi-. CROCKET. Can the minister say when Mr. Walberg received his last payment ? He was paid $100,221.91, up to the date of my asking the above question, and there was still outstanding a progress estimate amounting to $10,719. I would like to know when that was paid ?

I will have to get that information at another time for my hon. friend.
To increase accommodation at Truro, $105,000.
What is this for ?

The estimate is as follows :	Station, $85,000 ; yard, $168,000 ;
water service, $5,000 ; coal pocket, $3,000 ; ballast, $30,000 ; store. $12,000 ; office, $25,000 : small items, $30,000 ; grading, $51,000 ; freight house, $25,000.
What is the total cost and what is the total amount expended ?
The total amount expended at Truro, including everything, is $271,366.77. That is not on the work I have outlined, which will cost over $400,000.
How much of this vote will it take to complete it ?
Is the work under contract, let by tender, and, if so, who are the contractors ?
We are doing the yard work ourselves, and the coal pits have been let. The balance of the work has not yet been let.
What part of the work is done ?

Part of the yard north of the main line of the Pictou branch is done by ourselves. The water service is done by contract.
Mr. TAYLOR, Is the new station to be let by tender ?
It has not been tendered for yet, but it will certainly be let by tender.
Is it the intention of the minister to start the new station this year ?
The plans are being considered now. I do not know just what we shall be able to do this year, as the season is so late ; but it is not the intention to make a difference between places.

The reason I ask the hon. minister this question is that in 1904 I think it was. the government started to build a new engine house. The work was left until the eve of a general election. They did not know what site they were going to select. You did not know what site you were going to take and were forced to take a certain site which cost the country a considerable sum. In turning up the Auditor General's Report, I find that upwards of $220,000 was spent on that engine house. Of that amount over $80,000 was spent in excavating. What I would like to impress on the minister is that it would be far better to provide this new station before the general elections. He would get just as many votes out of it and so will I, If fortunate enough to run. While on my feet, I would like to impress on the minister the absolute necessity for better precautions on the crossings in Truro. I have a copy of a letter sent by a lawyer to the department claiming damages on account of an accident at a crossing there, in which two horses were killed but fortunately without any loss of human life. The cause of the accident was this. It was a dark and stormy night and there were no lights on the crossing. The town of Truro had written the denartment several times begging it to put two lights on this crossing, but the department neglected to do so. From what I understand, the lawyer for the department wrote the Truro people that the government will not pay this claim. I would 1 like the minister to look into the question.

There are no gates any way down there and it is a miracle that no lives have been lost.
Intercolonial Railway-increased accommodation at Springhill junction, $2,900.

This is for coal plant and hot water pumps.
Improvements at Amherst, $47,000.
This is for a station, $38,000, a concrete platform and an engine house. Estimated cost $59,500. The contract was given to Leblanc & Company, the lowest tenderers, after newspaper advertisements.
Why build an engine house at Amherst? It is not a division point.
We have two engines there, used for shunting in the yard.

Before you leave the Nova Scotia items, I desire to call attention to the fact that while I am pleased to see so many votes for increased accommodation along various sections of the Intercolonial Railway passing through that province, I regret that the good old county of Inverness, through which thirty-five miles of the road runs, is left out. My regret is that the minister, on his tour of inspection, did not have time to see that fine county in daylight, and most of all to see its requirements. There is a private company owned railway running along the county of Inverness, a distance of 61 miles. There are three thriving coal mining towns tributary to that road, together with about two-thirds of the area of the county of Inverness and its people. All the freight emanating from these mining towns and other parts of that county, together with the passenger traffic, passes, almost all of it, over the Intercolonial Railway. That other railway forms a junction with the Intercolonial Railway about a mile and a half or so from the Strait of Canso, or about a mile and a half from Point Tupper, one of the Intercolonial railway terminals. Every passenger-and this is what I desire to call attention to particularly-who leaves the county of Inverness by that road has to land in a swamp along the track of the Intercolonial Railway. The government, it would appear, took excellent care to make accommodation for the freight coming off the Inverness and Richmond Railway, but it left the passengers to shift for themselves, and they have to land, as I have said, about a mile and a half from the government station at Point Tupper. The attention of the late Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) was brought to this matter by myself, and he claimed that it was the duty of the private company to provide a shelter there for its passengers. The company, on the other hand, contend that they have their station in the town
of Hawkesbury, about one-quarter of a mile from this junction, and that the moment they land their passengers on the Intercolonial track they are Intercolonial passengers, and consequently they back their train right to their station in the town of Hawkesbury. I have been time and again on board the Intercolonial and taken the Inverness train to my home, and in the spring and winter I have seen twenty-five to thirty passengers, of both sexes, having to walk the whole length of the train in snow and slush to their knees and get to the Intercolonial as best they could. This has been going on some six or seven years, so that it is a case, as far as the people of Inverness are concerned, of being between the de'il and the deep sea. What I contend is that the passenger earnings which the Intercolonial derives from this traffic amply warrant a station being built at that junction by the government for their accommodation. The passenger earnings on this 61 miles of the Inverness railroad this last calendar year were $20,000, and no doubt that would be at least duplicated on the Intercolonial, because the run on that road is longer. With its freight traffic and passenger traffic that 01 miles of railway cleared $75,000 last year, as is shown by the government returns. These earnings, I say again, have been more than duplicated in the case of the Intercolonial, because the greater amount of that freight and traffic would go over the Intercolonial sometimes twice or three times the distance that it goes over the Inverness road. I listened to a question asked and answered in this House the other day as to the amount paid by the Sydney and Louisburg Company to the government for the use of the government terminals at Sydney. It is evident from that question and its answer that the Sydney and Louisburg road is compelled to make use of the government terminals at iSydney, for which they pay a certain amount. What I claim is then that it is the duty of the government either to erect a modest station for the shelter of the passengers here or compel the running of the Inverness trains into the government terminals at Point Tupper. The people of Inverness would be perfectly satisfied with either.
What is the distance to Point Tupper?

About a mile and a half. I think that the request I make of the government is perfectly reasonable. To show the absurdity of the present arrangement let me state the position as it is. A freight train to-day leaves Inverness town, goes to the junction and then right ou into the government terminals at Point Tupper, where it transfers its freight comfortably. But a train loaded with passengers leaves soon after and is treated very differently.

The passengers are dumped in a swamp, the most hideous looking place along the Intercolonial Railway.
I was determined, before these votes went through, to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to this matter, in order that at least, he should give the matter attention when the Supplementary Estimates are being prepared, or arrange with the company, as I have indicated, that they might use the government terminals at Point Tup-per. I certainly refuse to hold a seat in this House quietly and silently while this abuse of the people X represent goes on.
What do you think of that, Mr. Minister?

As 1 understand the hon. member (Mr. McLennan) the Canadian Northern, or Inverness road, put the passengers off at a place other than the station, landing them on the Intercolonial tracks. That is a matter well worth looking into; and, if my hon. friend will drop me a line putting the matter in concrete shape, I will take it up with the railway. Perhaps the Railway Commission might induce them to do something, or wre might make some arrangement with them.

There is an excellent way for the minister to arrange this matter perhaps better than in any other, and that is to make this excellent piece of railway a branch of the Intercolonial-to take it over and experiment with it as an excellent feeder of the road. I am introducing this subject to the attention of the minister with the hopeful assurance that the road cleared $75,000 in its working for the last calendar year.

I notice in the newspapers a statement that the Minister of Railways is expected to spend a month or two in inspecting the Intercolonial. While he is on that tour of inspection, I would like him to spend a few days in my county. The reaspn I ask is that we are sadly in need of branch railways. I will not weary the House or take up its time with a long discussion of these matters, but I would merely say that the branch railways particularly needed are from Brookfield to Lansdowne, Brule to Truro, and from Parrsboro' to Truro. The minister need not laugh at this. If he had [DOT]seen, as I saw last fall, the farmers and the merchants of that country having their stuff hauled over muddy roads-It was a muddy season-at a cost of $3 to $5 a ton, he Would have seen the need of these branch roads. And I believe it can be shown that the roads I have mentioned are a paying proposition. If the minister will spend a day or two *with me, we will look it over.
Improvements at Sackville, $27,000.

What are these improvements?
Mr. Mclennan.
Station, freight sheds, grading of track, water service and so on- total, $06,000.
Have the contracts been let?	'
The contract has been let for the station. Calls are out for the freight sheds, but tenders have not yet been received.
What was the contract for the water system?
Who was the contractor?
Willard, Kitchen & Co., Limited.
How much for the station?
The contractor is Thomas R, Anderson, at $20,000.

Speaking of stations, I do not want to repeat at length what I have already said in this House and privately to the minister, in regard to the need for a new station of the Intercolonial at Fredericton. The Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) who was acting Minister of Railways last session, admitted that Fredericton was entitled to a better station than we have now. The Minister of Railways has himself visited Fredericton anil seen the station, and both he and his deputy have admitted that the station is neither creditable to the railway nor to Fredericton, as the cap'tal of the province. I will simply say that the Fredericton people are looking to the Supplementary Estimates this year to find provision for a new7 building and that they will be grievously disappointed if no provision is made.

What is the total amount of these improvements? What will be required after this vote to complete
them ?
It is expected that this vote will complete the work. There is a revote here of $20,000. The total cost wTill be $66,000.
I would like to hear from the Minister of Railways as to the proposition to erect a new station at Fredericton.
They are not in these estimates.
I have noticed that.

I can say nothing further, except to recommend faith and hope for a few days.
Towards double tracking parts of line, $200,000.
What parts of the line are to be doubled track?
Prom Moncton to Pain-sec Junction.
What is your plan for double tracking the road? Has the minister looked over the southern road from Moncton to Halifax that he did not know whether he would adopt or not?

The double track is absolutely necessary on this piece to accommodate the traffic. This double track goes toward Prince Edward Island. The other question is a large one. If the trade of Canada is to come from the west and to be exported from Canadian ports, and the goods imported into Canadian ports at Halifax and St. John, they will have to be provided for. The Grand Trunk Pacific is near Moncton, the Canadian Pacific Railway' is now at St. John, - the Canadian Northern is at Quebec, and some way will have to be found to get this traffic from Moncton to St. John and Halifax, and somebody will have to provide more railway communication between Moncton and St. John and between Moncton and Halifax.

The Grand Trunk Pacific will not be finished until 1911, and it will require a couple ocf years to develop the traffic at least, so it will be thirteen years before the minister will have to take into consideration either the double tracking from Moncton or building this new line.

This question was discussed two or three years ago in this House. The policy was then laid down that the Intercolonial should be doubled tracked between St. John and Halifax, as early as circumstances would permit, and there were certain portions of the line which, if it were to meet present requirements, must necessarily be double tracked at once. For instaance, a double track was absolutely necessary between Halifax and Windsor Junction. That work was done, and also a double track was put down between Stel-larton and New Glasgow. At the same time there was a location made between Hampton and the city of St. John. That work I believe has not been commenced, although the surveys have been made. Within the very near future a double track will have to be extended on to Springhill. Between Moncton and Springhill the traffic to-day is very heavy indeed. One of the great difficulties in proceeding with the double track must necessarily be the grade between Dorchester and Sac-kville. Pursuant to that policy, the Department of Railways and Canals, as I understand, have been conducting surveys in order to obviate some of these difficulties. Therefore, this is not a new question, it is one which has been practically settled. In the very near future, and indeed before the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway reaches Moncton and seeks an outlet at Halifax, the necessities of the traffic between Moncton
and Truro and Truro and Halifax will make it absolutely necessary for the government to double track that portion of the Intercolonial.

I have taken two and a half years as the period for which interest would be charged. That I think is the usual practice. During the period of five years the interest charges will continually increase. During the first year they will be very small. During the last year they will be very large. The custom, as I understand, is to take one-half of the period of construction and estimate interest, at whatever the rate may be, for that period. So far as the rate is concerned I have taken the reply of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in the House today in which he says that a recent loan has been floated bearing interest at 31 per cent. That loan was underwritten at par. I have taken 3J per cent or 1 per cent below the rate on the loan, as a fair interest charge during the period of construction.
With respect to the interest during the seven years during which the Grand Trunk Pacific Company pay no rental, I have endeavoured to be very conservative in my estimate. The Grand Trunk Pacific agree to pay a rental of 3 per cent after seven years. It is highly probable that during that period of seven years the interest which the country will have to pay will be at least 3i per cent, and I think I would have been justified in making up the loss to the country during that period at that rate, but I have given the government and the transaction the benefit of the doubt, and I have made my estimate during that period at only 3 per cent, which is the rate of rental the Grand Trunk Pacific Company will eventually pay to the government.
I have observed the same course in making an estimate for the three years additional, computing the interest during those three years at 3 per cent and not at 3J per cent. I certainly do. I say it is an extraordinary thing for an engineer of the railway to assume the responsibility of entering into a contract of that magnitude without any instructions from the department. I doubt whether the department itself, until this House authorized an appropriation for the purpose, would have been warranted in entering into any contract. Much less was a subordinate official of the Intercolonial at Moncton authorized to prepare plans for this work, and enter into a contract, and set the contractor at work, under a verbal agreement, without having received any instructions from any official of the department, or even reporting the matter to the department down to the time that the deputy minister was examined a few weeks ago. How can you do that on schedule rates?

I only mention that as one of the methods by which it could be dealt with. There is a third method of dealing with it, and that is by force account. Any one acquainted with railway business knows that it is a method which is resorted to invariably by railway companies, because it is a fail-method. Take the amount actually expended by the contractor, and 15 per cent is a reasonable amount of profit, and is so recognized by railway co'mpanies everywhere in dealing with works of that kind. I do not understand that my hon. friend takes any objection to the method of dealing with it by force account, but merely that Mr. Mackenzie should not have done what he did. I would like to hear Mr. Mackenzie's explanation of that matter when he comes before the committee. I agree with my hon. friend that Mr. Mackenzie should not assume too much responsibility.
