This work was of that description.

The principle is this : When a contractor enters into a contract, if contracts are drawn up now as they used to be, he accepts responsibility for all the quantities made out by the department. If there is an error committed by the department there is a provision in the contract that before the contractor commences his work he has to get & written order from the chief engineer, and the chief engineer generally allows him, as the hon. member has stated, what has been the actual amount expended on the work plus 15 per cent. There can be but very little of that kind of work in the contract for the building of the ear shops, the locomotives and equipment.
The point is as to whether or not this sewer, which was necessary in consequence of the erection of the shops, should have been included in the original contract.

If this large expenditure is not included in the contract the engineer in chief, or the engineer in charge, has no right to let that work to the contractor. The proper way is to call for new tenders for the work. The contractor assumes the responsibility of the engineering and of the architecture of the building and the schedule price has only reference to the work under contract. If there has been a mistake made by the architect or tbe party who drew the plans for these buildings that must be corrected by the engineer and before the contractor does a cent's worth of work, or is entitled to anything, he must get an order from the engineer in his own hand writing. If there have been laige sums of money expended outside of the contract there is no justification at all for it.

What makes this thing look rather bad, in so far as thd engineer is concerned, is this: Here is an expenditure which is started. If there had been any payment on account of the work at all we would have been able to have had the matter brought up and properly investigated in the Public Accounts Committee.
Does my hon. friend blame the department or Mr. Mackenzie?

Mr. Mackenzie is an officer of the department and it was Mr. Mackenzie who made the mistake if a mistake was made. If moneys had been paid on it we would have been able to have investigated it in the Public Accounts Committee. When does the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) expect that the matter can be brought up in the Public Accounts Committee according to the rules of this House?
You have brought it up now.
I admit it is practically out of order.
Not out of order at all.
To bring it up in the Public Accounts Committee.
We have been very liberal in giving you the opportunity of going into all these matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As this is before the Public Accounts Committee perhaps it would be better to leave it there.

When we are discussing an item in the estimates, because that item is under consideration by the Public Accounts Committee, surely we are not to be prevented from discussing in the fullest possible manner any evidence which may have been adduced concerning it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe you can discuss everything in connection with the item but hardly what is going on before the Public Accounts Committee.
Why not? Can the evidence that is given in reference to this item not be discussed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Because the committee has not reported on that point.
It reports the evidence every day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand from the statements made that Mr. Mackenzie is still to be called before the committee. I just want to shorten the debate. You can discuss the item, but not what is going before the committee.

I never heard of a case in which a department had a contract going on, but what there were progress estimates made on account of the contract. The result of the way this is manipulated will be that it will be two years before that item -will appear in the Auditor General's Report, so that it can come up in the regular way in the Public Accounts Committee. Next session we will only be able to investigate what appears in the Auditor Gen-
Mr. ,f. D. REID.
eral's Report up to March 31, 1908. It is hardly fair in the interest of the public that tlie matter should be staved off so long. It is a very strange proceeding that the Department of Railways and Canals should allow an official of the department to give a contract outside of the original contract they gave, which will amount to anywhere from $20,000 to $50,000. The position, as I understand it, is that the officials can make contracts verbally without even advising the department. if the department undertake the erection of a building-take the Moncton car shops for instance-and if there are to be any extras or changes the minister should be made aware of what these changes are and what they are going to cost so that he can give orders as to how they are to be carried out. There is not a solitary contract on the Intercolonial Railway that has been carried out but what the amount has exceeded the contract price by a very large sum. I do not think that is the right way of doing business. If a man gives a contract to a private individual for a building he generally gets a statement of what the cost is to be and that is all he has to pay, but in so far as these works on the Intercolonial Railway are concerned, they exceed very much the amount of the estimate. If it is going on in this case how do we know that it is not going on in other cases?
When does the minister expect these works will be completed?
The contractor says in four months. If they are completed in six or eight months I will be satisfied.
We have not had an answer yet as to the total amount that has been spent.

I told the hon. gentleman in my first statement, that I had no statement from the contractor and had not paid him anything. With reference to that work and the position of the department and the chief engineer, my hon. friend must remember that the chief engineer is an old employee. Hs is not in the position of a subordinate, as you call him, although he is subordinate to the department. He is chief engineer of the Intercolonial Railway. He is a man of great experience, and when the contract was Jet for that building it was found necessary to have a very large drain constructed. At some places it runs to a depth of 24 feet. It was necessary for drainage purposes and in his wisdom he made this arrangement with the contractor who had all the appliances on hand. My hon. friend will see that we do not pay ith'e contractor anything on account of the work because there has never been any money voted up to the present time. The chief engineer thought it was wise to do this work immediately before the buildings were constructed and he started the construction

of this very large sewer for drainage purposes. If the accounts are kept properly and honestly I am prepared to say that this is as cheap a way as any of getting work of this kind done, and if it were my own I would be prepared to do it in that way.
New machinery for locomotive and car shops, $155,000.
Some of this goes into the new shops at Moncton and some into the other shops at Halifax, Riviere du Loup and other places.
Is this by public advertisement and tender ?
All the machinery is purchased by tender. We generally purchase from Th? large firms dealing in this.
Is any of it purchased in the United States ?

That has not been purchased yet. Sometimes we buy in the United States, but my object is to buy everything possible from our own Canadian people.
Rolling stock, $1,550,000.
This is for additional rolling stock, ten passenger and twenty-two freight locomotives, three shunting locomotives, 300 box cars and so on.
What firms are supplying the new locomotives ?
The passenger locomotives are purchased from the Montreal Company and the freights from the Canadian Company.
What is the price ?

The passenger engines cost $24,000, and the freight engines $21,950.
Increased accommodation at St. John, $120,-
000.
This is for ballasting, grading tracks, car repair shops, coal pockets, &c.
How much grain has passed through the government elevator there in the past year ?
I have not the figures, but I understand that a greater amount of grain has passed through this year than in any previous year.
Does the hon. gentleman intend to build a spur from the Intercolonial Railway near the wharf to Robertson's coal pockets at Robertson's wharf ?
I think we have not an amount in this year.

I think the coal company propose to build that themselves.
They get the permission of the Intercolonial Railway.
I understood the Intercolonial Railway would build it there and I presume expropriate the property to build it on.

There is a basis on which all such things are done. Unless there is some special reason the private individual does the grading and tie laying and the railway lays down the tracks and takes a certain amount on the cars handled In order to repay the expenditure. No special arrangement has been made with the coal company.
The minister has given the cost of increased accommodation at Halifax at about $4,000,000. What has the increased accommodation at St. John cost ?
We have spent at St. John up to March 31, 1907, $2,582,616.30.
Since when was that?

A good many years back. I will not say really from the beginning, but this is the amount given to me as the total expenditure at St. John.
To put railway between Indiantown and Blackville into condition for operation, $80,000.
Why was nothing done with this matter last year?
We could not get any contract to build the bridge there and the work was stopped. It was almost impossible in the early part of the year to get contracts.
When that is completed is it intended to make a connection with Fredericton by Newcastle and the Indiantown branch?

I would not like to say what the intention is.
Improvements at Campbellton, $25,000.

I would like to know what the policy of the department is in regard to purchasing coal cranes ; is it to be through a middleman or by contract? As I understand, you cannot buy in Canada the kind of cranes required for the Intercolonial Railway, and they have to be purchased from firms which the Intercolonial have been dealing with every year for the last ten or fifteen years. If we can buy other kinds of cranes from these firms, there is no reason why we cannot buy cranes for the coal business from them at less cost than he can buy them from a middleman.
They are bought by tender.

Does not the hon. gentleman know that the people from

whom they are bought are Canadian agents of the American manufacturers who alone make them? He calls them middlemen, because they happen to live in Canada.
The man from whom they were bought swore that he was not the agent of the firm that manufactured them.
That is one instance.
The government formerly always before purchased these cranes directly from the manufacturers except in one instance. I claim that if they do that they will save a lot of money.

It is not fair to call the agent of a manufacturing establishment a middleman, as if you were making some reflection upon him. If a letter were sent to the agent's firm in the United States they would probably send it back to him so as not to do him an injustice. I do not think it is at all disgraceful to be a representative of one of these large firms. In some instances the firm themselves have asked us 10 per cent more than they have allowed their agents to quote us. What my hou. friend would call a middleman is a respectable agent of the firm, and the firm stands by him and allows him to do the business.
. Mr. J. D. REID. I would like my hon. friend to show the case he mentions, for I never heard of such a case.
Ste. Rosalie,-Improvement at, $85,900.

We are making arrangements for a water supply, for an engine house, a building for stores, a turntable, grading, masonry, tracks, and ballasting. The engine house and the tanks are under contract and the building for stores. The engine house $20,000, building for stores $3,500.
Increased accommodation and facilities along the line, $169,000.
That is a large sum and the House should insist on a specific statement of how the money is spent.
A good deal is for additional sidings at different stations.

Hitherto these have been voted specifically. This is an exemplification of the absurdity of charging to capital account all tjiese little expenditures.
To strengthen bridges, $190,000.
When is this work to be finished ? We have this item every year.
It is work that has to be done. The strengthening of bridges is one of the most important things for the safety of the road and public. We did not spend anything last year.

This vote is for changing bridges which were not up to the standard. You changed your locomotives and got much heavier ones and then have to change your bridges so as to make them capable of bearing them. When will this be finished ?
We have really to go over the whole line, and there are one or two sections on the road that have not been really commenced.
Are these maps made in the Geological Survey branch or in the' same branch as the map making of the Interior department ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The map making of the Interior Department is separate alto-

gether from the Geological Survey. We have draughtsmen and map makers in the Geological Survey, and they do the work. In some of our work, we have the assistance of the photographers branch of which Mr. White is the head.
Who is the head of this department ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Senecal is the chief draughtsman.
To pay for specimens for Victoria Memorial Museum, $5,000.
Where are these specimens kept ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In the Geological Survey on Sussex street.
When is the new museum likely to be finished ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: What is the amount of the allowance to correspondents of the ' Labour Gazette ' ?
There are forty-five correspondents and each is paid at the rate of $100 per annum.
There is an increase in this vote of $2,350. What is the explanation of that ?

As the hon. gentleman knows we passed last year the Act providing for investigation into labour disputes. We had about forty cases last year, and happily, they were all settled under the new law. We have had to send Mr. King and other representatives of the department to preside over these boards of inquiry and that entailed some expenditure. But I trust that the country approves of the work of the department in that direction, as we were very successful in all our investigations.
Fisheries-salaries and disbursements of fishery inspectors, overseers and guardians, $137,600.
There is an increase of $10,000 in that vote. It is to provide for some new appointments in the Northwest and British Columbia and also some small increases in salaries to the officers.

We are willing to allow these items to run through without very
much discussion, reserving one, but with the right to discuss the whole vote.
All right, which one does the hon. gentleman wish to have reserved ?

The first one.
Lighthouse and coast service-construction cf lighthouses and aids to navigation, including apparatus, submarine signals and providing suitable boats for carrying on construction work in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and elsewhere in the Dominion, $260,000.
This item was left over out of the general lighthouse and coast service.
I think the minister ought to give some idea of what is to be done under this vote.

We discussed this item several times, and I gave the information concerning it. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) will remember that he asked that this item should stand, and that was agreed to, but we discussed it before.
Department of Marine and Fisheries-Magnetic observatory, $3,200; Meterological service $122,000; Montreal observatory, $500; Kingston observatory, $500; Hydrographic surveys, $170,000.
I presume it is under this item that observatories are being erected throughout the country. Is it the Department of Marine and Fisheries who are erecting these towers throughout the country?

That is not under the Meteorological service of my department.
Steamboat inspection, $13,000.

When does the minister intend to go with the Bill from the Senate in reference to steamboat inspection? There is a good deal of dissatisfaction on the lakes because the customs officers cannot deal with gasoline launches. Some of the customs officers say that they cannot do anything until it becomes law.
The Bill provides for that. In the meantime we do not enforce it.
When does the minister intend to bring up that Bill that has been on the Order Paper so long?

As soon as the more pressing work which is now demanding our attention has been disposed of. We want to send as much work as we can to the Senate.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions, $1,291,550.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to explain with regard to all these items that

in consequence of suggestions which were offered the previous session, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has published a supplement to his report which gives particulars of each one of these services and full explanations. This supplement has been in possession of hon. gentleman for some time, and those who feel an interest in the matter have given it their consideration. Information concerning each one of these services is fully set forth in this blue-book entitled ' Supplement to the Report of the Department of Trade and Commerce.'
Are these subsidies all the same as last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except in one case- the British ocean mail service-where there is an increase. That is due to the fact that the contract fixes a price that each vessel gets, and as we get more trips from the better vessels we necessarily have to pay them more. With the exception of that item, I think they are all the same as last year.
I would suggest that one item be reserved for discussion by the leader of the opposition or any other member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a reasonable proposition.
Will the minister agree that some time shall be fixed when the various supplementaries will come up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope to bring the supplementary estimates down to-morrow or the following day, at the latest, and from then to the end of the session I fancy that all business will receive expeditious treatment, so that it will hardly be necessary to fix a day.

A great many items are allowed to ship through on which there would naturally be some discusion if the members interested in them were present. But we do not want to sit here all the time waiting for some particular estimate to come up, and we would like to know when the supplementaries will be taken up.
Mi\ FIELDING. After the supplementaries come down, if any particular subject interests the hon. gentleman and he will notify us, we will either take up that item or fix a time for doing so.
Will the minister look at item 190 :	' Steam communication between St. John and ports in Cumberland basin, $3,000.' Is that subsidy paid to a steamer called the 'Harbinger?'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No contract has been entered into for this service. The subsidy was offered, but not taken up.
I beg to suggest that item 153 be reserved for discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very well. I wish to strike out item 169 : 1 Steam communication between a port or ports in Prince Edward Island and a port or ports in Great Britain, $7,000. A quarter of this sum has been voted, but we have no expectation that the service will be required, and practically the sum already voted will lapse. I move that we strike out the remainder, and in the supplementaries we will utilize the money for some other service suitable for Prince Edward Island.

Item 153 :	Ocean and
mail service between Great Britain and Canada, $550,000,' will stand, and any member of the opposition who wants to discuss any of the subsidies will have an opportunity of doing so under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I quite agree with what my hon. friend suggests.
Department of Trade and Commerce, $91,600.
How much money was paid to each of the provinces under the Chinese Immigration Act ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is practically all paid to British Columbia, but I will be able, when the matter comes up again, to give my hon. friend a more exact statement.
I think we had better let item 276 stand, as I see that it includes bounties on steel and iron.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not take in the bounties, but only covers the adminis-tx-ative expenses.
I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-All right. Let 276 stand.
Item allowed to stand.
Inspection of staples, $130,000.
Is it expected that other inspectors will be required in consequence of the amendments to the Grain and Inspection Acts; and, if so, will provision for these be made in the supplementary estimates ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The officer of the department says that the supplementaries will have to contain a further sum to cover that.
Will there be an item in the supplementary estimates for this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be some items, although I do not remember for what particular purpose.
Mi'. TAYLOR. And if we want to discuss anything in connection with the Department of Justice it may be discussed upon the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Penitentiaries, $559,050.
Will tliere be an Item in the supplemenary estimates for this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that on motions the matter of the Hodgins Committee comes up. After that the various government orders, Bills and resolutons might be taken up, and later in the day the balance of Supply.
The Minister of Militia said he had a statement to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would come in Supply, I presume. The Hodgins matter was arranged for the morning ; it would come on the motions.
Then Bills and Supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
It would be the Minis.-ter of Militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I understood it was arranged that he shall make a statement.
Either he or tile Minister of Railways, who has also a statement to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether the Minister of Railways will be ready on the Transcontinental matter.
Then it will be militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We take Militia and the balance of any items that may remain.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.38 p.m.
Wednesday, July 8, 1908.
